panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Same eye same patient active sympathetic ophthalmia case; color fundus shows posterior inflammatory changes with yellow-white spots consistent with multifocal choroiditis / Dalen-Fuchs spots. B: FA from same sympathetic ophthalmia eye showing active posterior inflammation with lesion-related hyperfluorescence indicating multifocal choroiditis activity. C: ICGA shows multiple hypocyanescent lesions of stromal choroidal involvement, classic for multifocal granulomatous choroiditis in sympathetic ophthalmia. D: FAF from same sympathetic ophthalmia eye showing RPE disturbance from active/chronic choroidal inflammation, sequelae of multifocal choroiditis. E: OCT from same case explicitly described as showing serous retinal detachment and choroidal thickening, both vocabulary findings for sympathetic ophthalmia.

panels.figure_caption: Multimodal imaging in sympathetic ophthalmia. Composite figure assembled from original images of representative cases of active sympathetic ophthalmia evaluated at IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy. (A) Ultrawidefield color fundus photograph showing posterior segment inflammatory changes compatible with sympathetic ophthalmia. (B) Fluorescein angiography demonstrating active posterior segment inflammation, including optic disc leakage and lesion-related hyperfluorescence. (C) Indocyanine green angiography showing multiple hypocyanescent choroidal lesions, consistent with stromal choroidal inflammatory involvement. (D) Fundus autofluorescence showing retinal pigment epithelium disturbance related to active or chronic inflammatory damage. (E) Optical coherence tomography demonstrating serous retinal detachment, choroidal thickening, and associated structural inflammatory changes. This figure illustrates the substantial multimodal imaging overlap between sympathetic ophthalmia and Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease; therefore, imaging supports activity assessment and follow-up, but the history of penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery remains essential for diagnosis. Composite figure assembled from original anonymized clinical images obtained from the same eye of the same patient evaluated at IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy. The panels illustrate complementary multimodal imaging findings from the same clinical case.

findings.label: Dalen-Fuchs spots at the retinal pigment epithelium
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Yellow-white subretinal spots (arrows) on clinical fundus photographs correspond to histopathological Dalen-Fuchs nodules'; in-text: 'Sub-RPE nodular lesions that appear yellow-white, corresponding to histopathologic Dalen-Fuchs nodules (Figure 1), are typical of sympathetic ophthalmia.'

panels.rationale: Single montage fundus photograph (no panel letters; treated as one panel A) of a human patient retina. The caption explicitly attributes the image to sympathetic ophthalmia and the arrows mark yellow-white subretinal spots that correspond to Dalen-Fuchs nodules, a classic manifestation. Prior caption triage also routes this as a real patient ophthalmic image to keep. No subtype is supported by the vocabulary or caption, and no age/ethnicity is stated. Only the directly captioned/visible Dalen-Fuchs spot finding is tagged; other in-text manifestations (mutton-fat KPs, vitritis, papilitis, exudative retinal detachment) are not shown in this fundus image and are not invented from context.

in_text_mentions: with mutton-fat keratic precipitates and moderate to severe vitritis, choroiditis, and papilitis in the posterior segment [11]. It is described that at initial onset, the main clinical findings such as optic nerve swelling and exudative retinal detachment are located in the posterior segment, while granulomatous anterior segment inflammation with mutton-fat keratic precipitates may be seen in severe and/or chronic recurrent cases [12-14]. findings.label: Dalen-Fuchs spots at the retinal pigment epithelium
findings.evidence: Histopathology of a Dalen-Fuchs nodule; caption and article title identify this as a manifestation of sympathetic ophthalmia

panels.rationale: Single H&E histopathology panel from a human patient showing a Dalen-Fuchs nodule (accumulation of macrophages beneath the retinal pigment epithelium). The caption explicitly names the Dalen-Fuchs nodule, the in-text ties it to sympathetic ophthalmia (25–35% of cases), and the article is dedicated to sympathetic ophthalmia. This is a specific, well-recognized histologic manifestation of the configured target disease, so the panel is included. No subtype is supported by the vocabulary; Dalen-Fuchs nodules are a classic feature. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is given.
panels.attribution_text: Chu and Chan. Sympathetic ophthalmia: to the twenty-first century and beyond.. Journal of ophthalmic inflammation and infection 2013. doi:10.1186/1869-5760-3-49. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathology of a Dalen-Fuchs nodule. There is an accumulation of mainly macrophages beneath the retinal pigment epithelium (brown color). Hematoxylin & eosin; original magnification, ×200.
in_text_mentions: Dalen-Fuchs nodules are a well-known feature of sympathetic ophthalmia that appears in 25% to 35% of cases [17]. They are primarily located in the choroid beneath the RPE or under the neuroretina. Dalen-Fuchs nodules undergo development, in which they are primarily composed of macrophages early on (Figure 2) but later may be composed of depigmented or degenerated RPE and a small number of lymphocytes [25,26].

panels.rationale: Single-panel high-definition spectral-domain OCT of the right eye in a case of sympathetic ophthalmia (caption and disease-focused article title). The figure comprises the infrared reference image with scan box (left) and the OCT B-scan (right) as one acquisition display, treated as a single panel per the no-panel-letter rule. The B-scan visibly shows hyporeflective serous detachment (white star) with an adjoining hyper-reflective RPE rip (white arrow), exactly as captioned. Serous/exudative retinal detachment is a recognized posterior manifestation of sympathetic ophthalmia and is captured by the allowed finding key; the RPE rip is a complication of the detachment and is absent from the vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. No subtype, stage, age, or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text mentions, so those fields are null/unknown; no skin is shown.

Caption and in-text explicitly attribute the fundus findings (macular scarring, peripheral chorioretinal scarring/atrophy, pigmentary macular changes) to Figure 2, and the image visibly shows a pale optic disc, macular pigmentary scarring, peripheral chorioretinal scarring and peripheral yellow-white RPE spots. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (1a, 1b). 1a: Slit-lamp photograph of the injured left eye in a case whose title and in-text course diagnose atypical sympathetic ophthalmia after trauma. The panel shows iris loss with iris pigment under the superonasal subconjunctival space and a centered IOL; this is not a normal eye or another disease, but it matches no configured vocabulary finding, so only proposed findings are listed. 1b: Slit-lamp photograph one month after injury shows complete loss of iris in the left injured eye. The in-text mention for Figure 1b links this eye to anterior chamber cells with iris loss in the setting of diagnosed atypical sympathetic ophthalmia; the granulomatous anterior uveitis vocabulary item is therefore tagged, while complete aniridia is kept as a proposed finding.

in_text_mentions: as no fundal view, B-scan ultrasonography of the injured eye was performed, which showed flat retina with no evidence of globe rupture.
